docs.title: Orchestration Engine
docs.text: A fault-tolerant, dependency-aware workflow orchestration engine for Python. Define tasks, dependencies, retries, and timeouts declaratively; supply the logic for each task; the engine schedules, executes, retries, times out, cancels dependents of failures, and records every state transition.

docs.title: Quick Installation
docs.text:
pip install orchestration-engine

For optional YAML workflow loading support: 

pip install "orchestration-engine[yaml]"

[!TIP] Modern Linux (PEP 668): If installing on Ubuntu 23.04+, Debian 12+, or Fedora without a global pip environment, activate a virtual environment first: 

python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install orchestration-engine

docs.title: Mission
docs.text:
Multi-step automation pipelines—such as AI agent workflows, ETL transformations, and distributed tool executions—frequently encounter transient network drops, rate limits, and unhandled worker crashes.

Orchestration Engine is designed to provide robust, deterministic workflow management with: - Zero runtime dependencies: Pure Python standard library implementation. - Durable persistence: Append-only SQLite audit trail recording all state transitions. - Crash resumption: Seamless resumption of interrupted runs without re-executing already-succeeded tasks. - Transparent concurrency: Deterministic execution scaling via threads or spawned isolated processes. - Fail-safe isolation: Faults in user task runners and lifecycle hooks never corrupt internal engine state.

docs.title: Core Features
docs.text:
• Dependency-Aware Scheduling: Tasks are scheduled as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) and advance as soon as all upstream dependencies succeed.
  • Automatic Retries & Exponential Backoff: Transient errors are retried according to a configurable RetryPolicy using exponential backoff: delay_seconds * 2**(attempt_count - 1).
  • Per-Task Timeouts: Asynchronously enforced deadlines abandon stalled threads or terminate spawned child worker processes.
  • Transitive Cancellation: When a task fails permanently, all downstream dependents (direct and indirect) are cancelled to a fixpoint, while independent branches continue executing to completion.
  • Data Flow: Tasks receive outputs from completed upstream dependencies via task.inputs, with automatic JSON serialization and persistence in SQLite Schema v2.
  • Lifecycle Hooks: Non-blocking callbacks (on_task_start, on_task_succeeded, on_task_failed, on_task_retry, on_workflow_done) for monitoring and logging.
  • Developer Ergonomics: Fluent WorkflowBuilder API, JSON and YAML workflow definitions, and a CLI tool (orchestration-engine).

docs.title: Production Use Cases
docs.text: See the full Use Cases Guide for architectural blueprints and complete implementations: - Multi-Step AI Agent Pipelines: LLM tool calling, retrieval, rate limit handling, and fan-in synthesis. - RAG Ingestion & Vector Indexing: Document chunking, concurrent embedding generation, and quality verification gates. - Automated Incident Triage & Remediation: Fan-out telemetry diagnostics, root-cause correlation, automated mitigation, and verification. - Resilient ETL Pipelines: Fluent DAG construction, type-safe data passing, and transactional SQLite persistence.

docs.title: Design Philosophy
docs.text:
1. Zero runtime dependencies: Everything is implemented using the Python standard library (sqlite3, multiprocessing, concurrent.futures, json, argparse).
  2. Correctness over raw throughput: Every state transition is written to SQLite before in-memory mutation occurs (write-ahead log).
  3. Small, cohesive internals: Each internal module has one job (scheduler, readiness, executor, transitions, runner, persistence, recovery, loader, builder).
  4. Minimal, frozen public API: Only explicitly approved symbols are exported in __all__.

Dataclass representing a discrete unit of work within a workflow.

    task_id: str
    name: str

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• OrchestrationError: Base exception for all errors raised by the engine.
  • WorkflowValidationError: Raised when DAG validation fails (cycles, missing dependencies, invalid timeouts/concurrency).
  • WorkflowDefinitionError: Raised when workflow definitions fail schema validation or contain malformed JSON/YAML.
  • PersistenceError: Raised when SQLite operations encounter a database error or file failure.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
orchestration-engine is designed around a single-writer architecture with strict separation of concerns across small internal modules.

                    +-----------------------------+
                    |       Public Client         |
                    | (run_workflow, resume_run)  |
                    +--------------+--------------+
                                   |
                                   v
                    +-----------------------------+
                    |         Coordinator         |
                    |   (Single-Writer Loop)      |
                    +--------------+--------------+
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                         |                         |
         v                         v                         v
+-----------------+       +-----------------+       +-----------------+
|   Readiness &   |       |  Worker Pool    |       |  Transitions &  |
|    Scheduler    |       | (Thread/Process)|       |   Persistence   |
+-----------------+       +-----------------+       +-----------------+
                                                             |
                                                             v
                                                    +-----------------+
                                                    | SQLite Database |
                                                    |  (WAL Mode)     |
                                                    +-----------------+

docs.title: Single-Writer SQLite Pattern
docs.text:
SQLite offers exceptional durability and zero-configuration storage, but concurrent multi-threaded writes can trigger sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked.

To eliminate SQLite locking issues completely: 1. Exclusive Coordinator Ownership: Worker threads and child processes never interact with the SQLite database. 2. Write-Ahead Transitions: The coordinator thread owns the SQLite connection. Before any in-memory state transition is applied, it writes the transition to the task_events audit table. 3. Connection Settings: - PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL: Write-Ahead Logging allows concurrent readers alongside writers. - PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL: Balances ACID guarantees with write speed. - PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON: Enforces relational integrity across tables. - PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000: 5-second automatic retry on internal lock contention.

docs.title: Execution Backends
docs.text: Workflows support three execution backends configured via executor:

docs.title: 1. Thread Backend (executor="thread")
docs.text:
• Backed by standard library ThreadPoolExecutor.
  • Low overhead, ideal for I/O-bound tasks (HTTP calls, database queries, LLM API calls).
  • On timeout: the worker thread future is abandoned by the coordinator. Python threads cannot be forcefully killed without native thread primitives.

docs.title: 2. Process Backend (executor="process")
docs.text:
• Uses multiprocessing.get_context("spawn") for complete memory and interpreter isolation.
  • Ideal for CPU-intensive tasks, untrusted user code, or tasks requiring true process termination.
  • Communicates task outputs and errors via unidirectional multiprocessing.Pipe.
  • On timeout: worker child process receives SIGTERM, followed by SIGKILL after a 0.2s grace period.
  • Requires that task_runner and inputs/outputs are picklable.

docs.title: 3. Inline Backend (executor="_inline")
docs.text:
• Internal deterministic execution backend used for testing.
  • Single-threaded, synchronous execution with fake time sources.

docs.title: Internal Module Map
docs.text: Module Responsibility models.py Core dataclasses: Task, Workflow, RetryPolicy, TaskResult, Hooks, TaskState, WorkflowStatus. readiness.py DAG dependency checks: determines ready tasks and detects blocked/cancelled tasks. scheduler.py schedule_once evaluation: advances ready tasks and cancels blocked dependents to a fixpoint. executor.py Task lifecycle dispatch: execute_task, complete_task, fail_task, retry_task. transitions.py State machine enforcement: validates legal state transitions and writes event logs. persistence.py SQLite schema migrations (v0 -> v1 -> v2), connection factory, and audit log queries. runner.py Coordinator loops (_run_coordinator_thread, _run_coordinator_process), timeout checking, retry sleep. status.py Status derivation: computes overall workflow status from in-memory or persisted task states. validation.py DAG cycle detection and configuration schema validation. loader.py File deserialization: loads workflows from JSON with JSON-pointer error collection, or YAML. builder.py Fluent WorkflowBuilder and round-trip workflow_to_dict serializer. cli.py Command-line interface subcommands (validate, run, resume, status, history, runs).

docs.title: Command-Line Interface (CLI) Reference
docs.text: The orchestration-engine package provides a standalone CLI tool for validating, executing, resuming, and inspecting workflow runs.

docs.title: Entry Points
docs.text:
The CLI can be invoked in two equivalent ways:

# As an installed console script
orchestration-engine <command> [options]

# As an executable Python module
python -m orchestration_engine <command> [options]

docs.title: Security & Runner Trust Model
docs.text:
The run and resume subcommands accept a --runner module:function flag.

[!WARNING] Specifying --runner dynamically imports Python code via importlib.import_module and executes the specified callable. To resolve local modules, the current working directory (os.getcwd()) is prepended to sys.path.

Running a workflow with --runner carries the same trust level as executing a Python script. Only pass runner paths from trusted sources.

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text:
All CLI commands follow strict, machine-parseable exit code contracts:

Exit Code Meaning Description 0 Success Workflow execution succeeded, or query/validation command succeeded. 1 Workflow Failure Workflow ran to completion but finished with status failed or cancelled. 2 Usage / Definition Error Invalid CLI arguments, schema validation failure, file not found, or run ID not found. 3 Internal / Database Error Database connection/query failure (PersistenceError) or unhandled runtime error.

docs.title: 1. validate
docs.text:
Validates a workflow definition file against the formal workflow schema. Supports JSON files, or YAML files if the optional yaml extra is installed (pip install 'orchestration-engine[yaml]').

orchestration-engine validate <workflow_file> [--json]

JSON Schema (--json): 

{
  "workflow_id": "wf-example-1",
  "tasks_count": 2,
  "valid": true
}

docs.title: 2. run
docs.text:
Executes a workflow to completion from a definition file.

orchestration-engine run <workflow_file> \
    --runner <module:function> \
    [--db <path>] \
    [--run-id <id>] \
    [--max-concurrency <N>] \
    [--executor <thread|process>] \
    [--json]
  • --runner: (Required) Path to the task runner callable in module:function syntax.
  • --db: Path to an SQLite database file. If omitted, an in-memory database is used.
  • --run-id: Optional custom identifier for the run. If omitted, a UUID is generated.
  • --max-concurrency: Maximum concurrent tasks (default: 1).
  • --executor: Concurrency backend: thread (default) or process.
  • --json: Output machine-readable JSON summary.

JSON Schema (--json): 

{
  "run_id": "477fdb0e0b774caf85cf4b6f80c47432",
  "workflow_id": "wf-example-1",
  "status": "succeeded"
}

docs.title: 3. resume
docs.text:
Resumes an interrupted or partially-failed workflow run from its persisted database state.

orchestration-engine resume <run_id> \
    --runner <module:function> \
    --db <path> \
    [--max-concurrency <N>] \
    [--executor <thread|process>] \
    [--json]
  • --db: (Required) Path to the SQLite database containing the persisted run.

JSON Schema (--json): 

{
  "run_id": "477fdb0e0b774caf85cf4b6f80c47432",
  "status": "succeeded"
}

docs.title: 4. status
docs.text:
Queries the current status of a workflow run from the database.

orchestration-engine status <run_id> --db <path> [--json]

JSON Schema (--json):

docs.title: 7. plan
docs.text:
Analyzes workflow structure and computes topological execution stages, critical path, and maximum parallelism without executing side effects.

orchestration-engine plan <file> [--json]
  • <file>: (Required) Path to the workflow JSON or YAML file.
  • --json: Format the execution plan output as structured JSON.

Example: 

orchestration-engine plan workflow.json

Output: 

Workflow: etl-pipeline
Total Tasks: 8
Max Parallelism: 4 concurrent workers
Critical Path: extract -> chunk -> embed -> index

Execution Stages:
  Stage 0: extract
  Stage 1: chunk_a, chunk_b, chunk_c, chunk_d
  Stage 2: embed
  Stage 3: index

docs.title: 8. dlq
docs.text:
Inspects and manages the persistent Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) for failed tasks.

orchestration-engine dlq <list|purge> [--db <path>] [--workflow <id>] [--limit <n>] [--older-than <sec>] [--json]
  • list: View captured task failure messages, stack traces, and input payloads.
  • purge: Delete captured failure messages matching filters.
  • --db: Path to the SQLite database (defaults to orchestration.db).
  • --workflow: Filter messages by workflow identifier.
  • --limit: Maximum number of messages to list (default: 50).
  • --older-than: Purge messages older than $N$ seconds.
  • --json: Output as structured JSON.

docs.title: 9. trace
docs.text:
Exports run execution spans into Google Chrome Trace Event Format (compatible with chrome://tracing and Perfetto UI).

orchestration-engine trace <run_id> --db <path> [-o trace.json]
  • run_id: Workflow run identifier.
  • --db: Path to the SQLite database.
  • -o, --output: Optional output JSON file path (defaults to stdout).

docs.title: 10. signal
docs.text:
Delivers a human-in-the-loop approval or external webhook payload to a workflow run.

orchestration-engine signal <run_id> <signal_name> [--payload <json>] [--db <path>]
  • run_id: Workflow run identifier.
  • signal_name: Identifier of the signal (e.g. approval, webhook, review).
  • --payload: JSON payload string (defaults to {}).
  • --db: Path to the SQLite database.

docs.title: 11. coordinator
docs.text:
Launches the zero-dependency distributed HTTP coordinator server. Orchestrates remote task polling, heartbeats, and run completion reporting across multiple worker agents over HTTP.

orchestration-engine coordinator [--host <host>] [--port <port>] [--db <path>]
  • --host: Host address to bind (default: 0.0.0.0).
  • --port: Port number to listen on (default: 9100).
  • --db: Path to SQLite database (defaults to orchestration.db).

docs.title: 12. worker
docs.text:
Launches an autonomous distributed worker daemon that connects to a remote coordinator over HTTP, polls available tasks, executes them, and streams back heartbeat status and completion payloads.

orchestration-engine worker --coordinator <coordinator_url>
  • --coordinator: (Required) Coordinator HTTP endpoint (e.g. http://127.0.0.1:9100).

docs.title: Observability & Logging
docs.text:
By default, the orchestration_engine library attaches a NullHandler to avoid hijacking parent application logs.

When running via the CLI, use the --log-level flag to enable structured standard logging:

orchestration-engine --log-level INFO run examples/simple_workflow.json --runner examples.runners:run

Supported log levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR.

Structured log events emit structured extra fields: - workflow_id: Workflow identifier - run_id: Run identifier - task_id: Task identifier - old_state: Previous task state - new_state: Next task state - attempt: Current attempt counter

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: This section provides an in-depth reference for the engine's scheduling, state management, fault-tolerance mechanisms, and persistence.

docs.title: Task Lifecycle and States
docs.text:
Each task within a workflow exists in one of seven well-defined states:

            +-------------+
            |   PENDING   |
            +------+------+
                   |
         +---------+---------+
         |                   | (dependency failure)
         v                   v
     +-------+         +-----------+
     | READY |         | CANCELLED |
     +---+---+         +-----------+
         |
         v
    +---------+
    | RUNNING |
    +----+----+
         |
    +----+-------------------+
    |            |           |
    v            v           v
+-----------+ +------------+ +--------+
| SUCCEEDED | | RETRY_WAIT | | FAILED |
+-----------+ +-----+------+ +--------+
                    |
                    v (delay expires)
                +-------+
                | READY |
                +-------+
State Description PENDING Initial state. Waiting for upstream dependencies to complete. READY All direct upstream dependencies have completed with SUCCEEDED. Task is eligible for dispatch. RUNNING Task has been assigned to an active worker thread or child process. SUCCEEDED Task runner returned success (True or TaskResult(ok=True)). Terminal state. RETRY_WAIT Task failed an attempt, but remaining attempts exist. Waiting for next retry deadline. FAILED Task exhausted all configured retry attempts. Terminal state. CANCELLED An upstream dependency failed or was cancelled. Dependent task is pruned. Terminal state.

docs.title: Scheduling and Readiness
docs.text: Scheduling operates on a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG): 1. DAG Validation: On workflow initialization or load, cycle detection (get_workflow_validation_error) ensures there are no circular dependencies and all dependency IDs exist. 2. Readiness Evaluation: A task transitions from PENDING to READY if and only if every task ID in its dependencies list is currently in SUCCEEDED state. 3. Execution Ordering: Ready tasks are dispatched as worker slots become available up to max_concurrency.

docs.title: Retries and Exponential Backoff
docs.text: When a task fails (by returning False, returning TaskResult(ok=False), raising an unhandled exception, or timing out): - If attempt_count < retry_policy.max_attempts: - The task transitions to RETRY_WAIT. - The next retry timestamp is calculated using exponential backoff: $$\text{delay} = \text{delay_seconds} \times 2^{\text{attempt_count} - 1}$$ - The coordinator sleeps until the earliest pending RETRY_WAIT deadline before checking for ready tasks. - If attempt_count >= retry_policy.max_attempts: - The task transitions to FAILED.

docs.title: Failure Propagation & Transitive Cancellation
docs.text:
When a task transitions to FAILED, any downstream task depending on it cannot succeed.

To maintain workflow integrity without hanging: 1. All direct dependents of a failed or cancelled task are transitioned to CANCELLED. 2. The cancellation algorithm runs to a fixpoint inside schedule_once, ensuring transitive dependents (e.g. A -> B -> C) are cancelled immediately within the same iteration. 3. Independent DAG branches are unaffected and continue running to completion.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text: Every task can specify a timeout_seconds: float | None (defaulting to 30.0s, or the workflow's default_timeout_seconds): - In the Thread backend: When a task exceeds its deadline, the coordinator marks the attempt timed out, schedules a retry or failure, and abandons the worker future. - In the Process backend: The coordinator terminates the child process (SIGTERM), waits for a brief grace period, and forcefully kills (SIGKILL) if unresponsive.

docs.title: Data Flow & Task Outputs
docs.text:
Tasks can pass structured data downstream: - Return TaskResult(ok=True, output={...}) from a task runner. - The output payload is validated as JSON-serializable and written to the SQLite task_outputs table. - Before executing a downstream task, the engine populates task.inputs with a dictionary mapping each dependency's task_id to its produced output: 

# In task 'calculate_tax' which depends on 'get_cart':
cart = task.inputs["get_cart"]

docs.title: Lifecycle Hooks
docs.text:
Lifecycle hooks allow applications to observe workflow execution without polling or mutating engine state: - on_task_start(task: Task): Invoked when a task enters RUNNING. - on_task_succeeded(task: Task): Invoked after a task completes successfully. - on_task_failed(task: Task): Invoked after a task exhausts retries and enters FAILED. - on_task_retry(task: Task): Invoked when a task attempt fails and enters RETRY_WAIT. - on_workflow_done(workflow: Workflow, status: WorkflowStatus): Invoked after all tasks reach terminal states.

All hooks are executed post-persistence. Any unhandled exception within a hook is caught and suppressed, guaranteeing that observer failures cannot crash workflow execution.

docs.title: 1. When should I choose the Thread backend vs the Process backend?
docs.text:
• Use Thread backend (executor="thread") for I/O-bound workflows such as HTTP requests, database queries, and AI model API calls. Threads have lower scheduling overhead and allow passing non-picklable in-memory objects.
  • Use Process backend (executor="process") when executing CPU-bound calculations, when isolating memory between worker tasks is required, or when hard termination of timed-out tasks (SIGTERM / SIGKILL) is essential.

docs.title: 2. How does resume work after a server crash?
docs.text:
When a process crashes or receives SIGKILL, incomplete tasks remain in RUNNING status in the SQLite database.

Upon calling resume_run(conn, run_id, task_runner, ...): 1. The engine scans the database for the given run_id. 2. Tasks that were RUNNING are marked as interrupted attempts and transitioned to RETRY_WAIT (if attempts remain) or FAILED. 3. Already SUCCEEDED tasks are preserved and never re-executed; their stored outputs in task_outputs are re-injected into downstream tasks. 4. The coordinator resumes scheduling from the exact point of interruption.

docs.title: 3. How does the engine avoid SQLite lock errors under concurrency?
docs.text: SQLite allows multiple readers but only one writer at any given moment. orchestration-engine uses a single-writer architecture: - Worker threads and child processes execute user code only and never connect to SQLite. - Only the main coordinator thread holds an SQLite connection and performs writes. - SQLite is initialized with PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL and PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000. - As a result, sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked cannot occur during normal execution.

docs.title: 4. Can tasks pass non-JSON data downstream?
docs.text: Task outputs stored in the database via TaskResult(ok=True, output=...) must be JSON-serializable to ensure that runs can be safely persisted, inspected by the CLI, and resumed from disk across process restarts. If a runner returns non-JSON serializable output, the attempt fails with an explanatory error.

docs.title: 5. What happens if a lifecycle hook raises an exception?
docs.text: Lifecycle hooks (Hooks) run immediately after state transitions have been committed to SQLite. Any exception raised by a hook callable is safely caught and suppressed by the engine (_safe_call_hook). This ensures that failures in metrics or notifications never corrupt internal state or disrupt pipeline execution.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: orchestration-engine requires Python 3.12 or higher and has zero runtime dependencies in its core installation.

docs.title: Known Limitations & Design Boundaries
docs.text:
orchestration-engine prioritizes simplicity, correctness, and zero runtime dependencies over multi-node distributed complexity.

The following known limitations and non-goals are deliberate design trade-offs:

docs.title: 1. Thread Timeouts Cannot Forcefully Terminate Threads
docs.text:
In the Thread backend (executor="thread"): - When a task reaches its timeout_seconds, the coordinator marks the task attempt as timed out, schedules a retry or failure, and moves forward. - However, standard Python threads cannot be forcefully killed from the outside without unsafe native CPython hacks. - If a thread is stuck inside a blocking C call (e.g., an uncooperative network socket without a socket-level timeout), the underlying thread will remain alive until it returns or the process exits.

Mitigation: Use executor="process" if hard termination via SIGTERM / SIGKILL is strictly required.

docs.title: 2. Single-Node Execution (No Distributed Coordination)
docs.text:
• orchestration-engine coordinates tasks on a single machine using SQLite and local processes or threads.
  • It does not support multi-machine scheduling (e.g., Celery, Airflow, Temporal, Ray).
  • It does not integrate with message brokers (RabbitMQ, Kafka, Redis).

docs.title: 3. SQLite Single-Writer Bottleneck
docs.text:
• While WAL mode enables high write throughput, all transitions route through the single coordinator loop.
  • The engine is optimized for multi-step AI and data pipelines where task duration ranges from hundreds of milliseconds to minutes, rather than millions of micro-tasks per second.

docs.title: 4. No Built-In Cron Scheduler or Web UI
docs.text:
• The engine provides on-demand execution and resume via Python APIs and the CLI.
  • Recurring cron schedules, backfilling, and web dashboards are out of scope and should be handled by external schedulers (e.g., systemd timers, cron, GitHub Actions).

docs.title: Performance & Benchmarks
docs.text:
This document records baseline performance metrics for orchestration-engine, including scheduling latency, SQLite audit log write throughput, and multi-worker concurrency scaling.

[!NOTE] Benchmarks measure engine overhead and durability performance. They are not run as assertions in continuous integration. To reproduce these measurements, run: 

python -m benchmarks.run_all

docs.title: Environment Details
docs.text:
• Operating System: Linux 7.0.0-38-generic (x86_64)
  • Python Runtime: CPython 3.12.13
  • CPU Architecture: 24 Logical Cores (x86_64)
  • Storage: SSD (ext4)

docs.title: 1. Scheduling Overhead per Task
docs.text:
Measures the single-writer coordinator loop scheduling overhead and write-ahead state machine transition latency across a linear chain of 500 no-op tasks:

Metric Measured Value Total Tasks 500 Total Wall-Clock Time 0.3136 s Average Latency per Task 627.23 µs Scheduling Throughput 1,594.3 tasks / second

Analysis: Average scheduling overhead per task is under 1 millisecond (~0.62ms), making coordinator overhead negligible compared to typical real-world I/O or LLM response times (100ms - 5000ms).

docs.title: 2. Event-Log Write Throughput
docs.text:
Measures append-only event-log write speed to an on-disk SQLite database configured with Write-Ahead Logging (PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL) and PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL:

Metric Measured Value Events Logged 1,000 Total Time 0.0224 s Average Write Latency 22.36 µs Write Throughput 44,730.5 writes / second

Analysis: WAL mode achieves over 44,000 durable write operations per second, confirming that SQLite write-ahead logging does not bottleneck single-node workflows.

docs.title: 3. Concurrency Scaling
docs.text:
Measures wall-clock time executing 16 independent tasks (each task sleeping for 50ms) across varying worker concurrency levels using ThreadPoolExecutor:

Concurrency (max_concurrency) Wall-Clock Time (s) Effective Speedup Scaling Efficiency 1 0.8105 s 1.00x 100% 2 0.4077 s 1.99x 99.4% 4 0.2044 s 3.97x 99.1% 8 0.1031 s 7.86x 98.2%

Analysis: The engine exhibits near-linear speedup as max_concurrency scales from 1 to 8 workers, demonstrating near-zero lock contention in the coordinator dispatch loop.

docs.title: 1. Semantic Versioning
docs.text:
orchestration-engine strictly adheres to Semantic Versioning 2.0.0:

$$\text{MAJOR}.\text{MINOR}.\text{PATCH}$$

  • PATCH (1.0.x): Backwards-compatible bug fixes, documentation enhancements, and internal performance optimizations. No API changes.
  • MINOR (1.x.0): Backwards-compatible feature additions, additive schema migrations, and formal deprecation announcements.
  • MAJOR (x.0.0): Breaking API changes, backward-incompatible schema shifts, or removal of previously deprecated interfaces.

docs.title: 2. Definition of Public API
docs.text: Only symbols explicitly declared in orchestration_engine.__all__ and the CLI interface documented in docs/cli.md constitute the public contract:

docs.title: Public Symbols (orchestration_engine.__all__)
docs.text:
• Core Models: Task, Workflow, RetryPolicy, TaskResult, Hooks, TaskState, WorkflowStatus
  • Execution & Persistence: run_workflow, run_workflow_from_file, resume_run, get_connection, get_run_status, get_run_history, get_workflow_status, get_workflow_history, list_runs
  • Builder & Loaders: WorkflowBuilder, workflow_to_dict, load_workflow_from_json, load_workflow_from_yaml
  • Exceptions: OrchestrationError, WorkflowDefinitionError, WorkflowValidationError, PersistenceError
  • Metadata: __version__

[!IMPORTANT] All other internal modules (orchestration_engine.readiness, orchestration_engine.scheduler, orchestration_engine.transitions, etc.) are private implementation details and are subject to change without notice.

docs.title: 3. Deprecation Policy
docs.text: When an existing public interface, parameter, or behavior is superseded: 1. Notice Period: The interface will be marked deprecated for at least one full minor release cycle prior to any removal. 2. Runtime Warning: The interface will emit a Python DeprecationWarning to alert callers. 3. Changelog: Deprecations are highlighted prominently in CHANGELOG.md under a dedicated ### Deprecated header. 4. Removal: Deprecated interfaces may only be removed in a subsequent MAJOR version release.

docs.title: 4. task_states Deprecation Status
docs.text:
In early releases (v0.1.0), run_workflow required callers to provide a mutable dictionary to track task execution states:

run_workflow(workflow, task_states, time_source, task_runner, conn)

docs.title: Current Status
docs.text:
• Starting in v0.3.0, the internal engine was refactored to treat Task.state on the Task dataclass objects as the single source of truth.
  • The task_states dictionary is automatically synchronized as a mirror for full backwards compatibility with legacy callers.
  • Callers may safely pass an empty dictionary {} to run_workflow.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
• task_states remains accepted throughout all 1.x releases without breaking existing code.
  • In 2.0.0, task_states will be made optional or deprecated in favor of reading states directly from workflow.tasks.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This guide demonstrates defining a workflow, executing it in Python, and inspecting the resulting database audit log.

docs.title: 1. Define a Workflow
docs.text: Workflows can be defined in JSON, YAML, or programmatically using WorkflowBuilder.

docs.title: Option A: JSON Definition (workflow.json)
docs.text:
{
  "workflow_id": "wf-quickstart",
  "name": "Data Pipeline",
  "description": "Fetch, transform, and load pipeline",
  "default_timeout_seconds": 30.0,
  "tasks": [
    {
      "task_id": "fetch",
      "name": "Fetch API Data",
      "description": "Retrieves remote records",
      "dependencies": [],
      "retry_policy": {
        "max_attempts": 3,
        "delay_seconds": 1.0
      },
      "timeout_seconds": 15.0
    },
    {
      "task_id": "process",
      "name": "Process Records",
      "description": "Transforms retrieved records",
      "dependencies": ["fetch"],
      "retry_policy": {
        "max_attempts": 1,
        "delay_seconds": 0.0
      },
      "timeout_seconds": 30.0
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Option B: Programmatic Fluent Builder
docs.text:
from orchestration_engine import WorkflowBuilder, RetryPolicy

workflow = (
    WorkflowBuilder("wf-quickstart", "Data Pipeline")
    .description("Fetch, transform, and load pipeline")
    .default_timeout(30.0)
    .task(
        "fetch",
        name="Fetch API Data",
        retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3, delay_seconds=1.0),
        timeout_seconds=15.0,
    )
    .task(
        "process",
        name="Process Records",
        dependencies=["fetch"],
    )
    .build()
)

docs.title: 2. Implement the Task Runner
docs.text:
A task runner is a callable that accepts a Task and returns either a bool (legacy) or a TaskResult:

from orchestration_engine import Task, TaskResult

def task_runner(task: Task) -> TaskResult:
    print(f"Executing: {task.name} ({task.task_id})")

    if task.task_id == "fetch":
        # Return output payload to downstream tasks
        return TaskResult(ok=True, output={"records": [1, 2, 3]})

    elif task.task_id == "process":
        # Upstream outputs are automatically injected in task.inputs
        records = task.inputs["fetch"]["records"]
        total = sum(records)
        return TaskResult(ok=True, output={"total": total})

    return TaskResult(ok=False, error="Unknown task")

docs.title: 3. Run the Workflow
docs.text:
import time
from orchestration_engine import get_connection, run_workflow, get_run_status

# Open or create SQLite persistence database
conn = get_connection("pipeline.db")

# Run workflow
run_id = run_workflow(
    workflow=workflow,
    task_states={},
    time_source=time.time,
    task_runner=task_runner,
    conn=conn,
    max_concurrency=2,
)

# Check run status
status = get_run_status(conn, run_id)
print(f"Run {run_id} finished with status: {status.value}")

docs.title: 4. Inspecting via the CLI
docs.text:
You can inspect the resulting database using the CLI:

# View run status
orchestration-engine status <run_id> --db pipeline.db

# View transition audit history
orchestration-engine history <run_id> --db pipeline.db

# List all recorded runs
orchestration-engine runs --db pipeline.db

docs.title: Real-World Use Cases
docs.text:
The Orchestration Engine is designed to provide zero-dependency, fault-tolerant execution for workflows where steps depend on each other, fail transiently, and require an auditable history.

Below are core production architectures implemented using the engine.

docs.title: 1. Multi-Step AI Agent Pipelines
docs.text:
Example Implementation: examples/agent_pipeline.py

Modern AI agent workflows often comprise multiple stages: knowledge retrieval, model inference, tool execution, critique/verification, and final synthesis.

flowchart TD
    retrieve["1. Retrieve Context<br/>(Vector DB / Tool)"] --> summarize["2A. Summarize<br/>(LLM Call with 429 Retry)"]
    retrieve --> extract["2B. Extract Entities<br/>(Structured Output)"]
    summarize --> report["3. Fan-in Executive Report<br/>(Synthesis Gate)"]
    extract --> report

docs.title: Key Engineering Patterns
docs.text:
• Transient Provider Retries: LLM APIs commonly return HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) or 503 (Overloaded). Configured RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3, delay_seconds=1.0) retries with exponential backoff.
  • Concurrent Fan-Out: Independent steps (e.g., entity extraction and narrative summarization) run concurrently via max_concurrency=2.
  • Data Flow: Step outputs (TaskResult(ok=True, output=...)) are stored in SQLite and automatically injected into downstream tasks via task.inputs.
  • Crash Recovery: If the agent host terminates abruptly mid-run, resume_run(conn, run_id, ...) resumes execution without re-executing completed tasks.

docs.title: 2. RAG Document Ingestion & Vector Indexing
docs.text:
Example Implementation: examples/rag_document_indexer.py

Building retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) indexes requires ingesting source documents, chunking text, computing vector embeddings, and indexing them into a vector database with strict quality verification.

flowchart LR
    fetch["fetch-docs<br/>(Load Documents)"] --> chunk["chunk-docs<br/>(Semantic Chunker)"]
    chunk --> embed["embed-chunks<br/>(Embedding API + Retry)"]
    embed --> index["index-vectors<br/>(Vector DB Upsert)"]
    chunk --> eval["evaluate-coverage<br/>(Fan-in Quality Gate)"]
    index --> eval

docs.title: Key Engineering Patterns
docs.text:
• Structured Data Propagation: The chunker splits documents and passes structured chunks downstream via task.inputs["fetch-docs"].
  • API Backpressure Mitigation: Embedding models frequently impose tight token rate limits. Automatic retry policies ensure zero lost data during network or provider hiccups.
  • Fan-in Evaluation Gate: evaluate-coverage compares the count of chunks produced by chunk-docs against the count of embeddings stored by index-vectors, validating indexing health before marking the workflow succeeded.

docs.title: 3. Automated Incident Triage & Remediation (DevOps / SRE)
docs.text:
Example Implementation: examples/incident_triage.py

Autonomous incident response systems must ingest alerts, run parallel diagnostics across different telemetry backends, synthesize a root-cause analysis (RCA), execute automated remediation, and verify recovery.

flowchart TD
    alert["1. Ingest Alert<br/>(Webhook / PagerDuty)"] --> logs["2A. Scan Logs<br/>(Search Stack Traces)"]
    alert --> metrics["2B. Inspect DB Pool<br/>(Check Saturation)"]
    alert --> deps["2C. Ping Dependencies<br/>(Health Checks)"]
    logs --> rca["3. Synthesize RCA<br/>(Multi-source Correlation)"]
    metrics --> rca
    deps --> rca
    rca --> remediate["4. Apply Mitigation<br/>(Resize Pool / Reset Conns)"]
    remediate --> verify["5. Verify Health<br/>(Confirm Nominal Error Rate)"]

docs.title: Key Engineering Patterns
docs.text:
• High Concurrency Diagnostics: Runs parallel checks against logs, metrics, and microservices simultaneously (max_concurrency=3).
  • Multi-Source Correlation: synthesize-rca aggregates diagnostic data from all 3 independent branches to isolate the true root cause.
  • Fail-Safe Transitive Cancellation: If automated mitigation fails, dependent verification steps are automatically CANCELLED, preventing premature incident closure.
  • Real-Time SRE Notifications: User-supplied Hooks notify operations channels (e.g. Slack, PagerDuty) upon step transition or retry without blocking the coordinator.

docs.title: 4. Resilient ETL & Data Processing Pipelines
docs.text:
Example Implementation: examples/builder.py and examples/data_flow.py

Data pipelines requiring strict transactional guarantees, schema migration, and zero data loss.

docs.title: Key Engineering Patterns
docs.text:
• Fluent Declarative Construction: Construct complex DAGs cleanly with WorkflowBuilder: 
    workflow = (
    WorkflowBuilder("etl-pipeline", default_timeout_seconds=30.0)
    .task("extract", timeout_seconds=10.0)
    .task("transform", dependencies=["extract"], max_attempts=3)
    .task("load", dependencies=["transform"])
    .build()
)
  • Portable Serialization: Round-trip workflows to JSON/YAML dictionaries via workflow_to_dict() and load_workflow_from_json().
  • Transactional State Persistence: SQLite write-ahead logging (WAL) logs all task events (task_events) and payloads (task_outputs) atomically.

docs.title: ADR 001: Non-Blocking Task Timeouts in Coordinator
Context
docs.text: In v0.1.0, task execution wrapped individual tasks inside with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as pool:. When a task exceeded its timeout_seconds, future.result(timeout=...) raised TimeoutError, but exiting the with block blocked the engine until the underlying thread finished execution. Consequently, a hung task with a 1-second timeout blocked the entire engine for the full duration of the hung task.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Replace the blocking context manager with an explicit ThreadPoolExecutor. When a timeout or task completion occurs, call pool.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True) in a finally block. Because Python threads cannot be preemptively killed from outside without terminating the process, the task thread will continue in the background, but the engine coordinator immediately marks the task failed and proceeds with scheduling other tasks.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Engine scheduling is no longer blocked by slow or hung tasks.
  • Background threads continue running until completion or process termination, which is documented as a known Python runtime constraint.

docs.title: ADR 002: Exception Handling and Retry Path Unification
Context
docs.text: In v0.1.0, when a task_runner threw an unhandled exception, run_workflow caught it and immediately transitioned the task to TaskState.FAILED directly via transition_task. This bypassed fail_task, ignoring the configured retry_policy.max_attempts, leaving task_states stale (still READY), and losing the exception details.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Route exceptions through fail_task, the same path taken when task_runner returns False. If attempts remain below max_attempts, the task enters TaskState.RETRY_WAIT with exponential backoff. Store the error on Task.last_error as "ExceptionType: message" (truncated to 2000 characters). For timeouts, store "timeout after Ns".

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Exceptions are retried like transient failures.
  • task_states remains synchronized with task.state.
  • Diagnostic failure details are captured on the task for inspection and history logs.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: v0.1.0 raised generic standard library exceptions (principally ValueError) for malformed workflow JSON, dependency cycles, duplicate task IDs, and raw sqlite3.Error on database failures. Callers had no type-safe way to catch engine-specific errors.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Introduce a structured exception hierarchy under OrchestrationError: - WorkflowDefinitionError(OrchestrationError, ValueError): Raised by loader.py when definitions lack required keys or have invalid types. - WorkflowValidationError(OrchestrationError, ValueError): Raised by runner.py when workflow DAGs contain cycles, self-dependencies, or missing dependencies. - PersistenceError(OrchestrationError): Raised when SQLite operations fail during connection creation, state transition writes, or history retrieval, chaining from e to preserve original DB error contexts.

Subclassing ValueError for definition and validation errors preserves backward compatibility with existing exception handlers.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Callers can catch specific orchestration errors or catch OrchestrationError broadly.
  • Existing code catching ValueError continues to function uninterrupted.
  • Database errors do not leak implementation-specific SQLite details unless explicitly inspected via __cause__.

docs.title: ADR 004: Schema v1 Migration and Runs Table
Context
docs.text: In v0.1.0/v0.2.0, the SQLite database had an unversioned task_events table lacking run isolation. Repeated runs of a workflow with the same workflow_id interleaved events in the same audit stream without distinction. Additionally, connection options (WAL mode, timeouts) were unconfigured.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Introduce schema versioning using SQLite's PRAGMA user_version = 1.
  2. Add columns run_id TEXT, next_retry_at REAL, and error TEXT to task_events.
  3. Provide automated, transactional, and idempotent migration (_migrate_database) from version 0 to version 1:
  4. Assign legacy events run_id = 'legacy-' || workflow_id.
  5. Create runs(run_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, workflow_id TEXT NOT NULL, started_at REAL NOT NULL, finished_at REAL, status TEXT NOT NULL, definition_json TEXT NOT NULL).
  6. Create indexes on task_events(run_id, id) and task_events(workflow_id).
  7. Configure connection pragmas for file databases: journal_mode = WAL, synchronous = NORMAL, foreign_keys = ON, busy_timeout = 5000 (skipping WAL for :memory:).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every run is isolated and searchable by run_id.
  • Backwards compatibility is preserved for v0 databases and test fixtures.
  • Concurrent reads and writes to SQLite file databases are robust against locking timeouts.

docs.title: ADR 005: Run Model and Lifecycle Tracking
Context
docs.text: Orchestrating workflow executions across multiple attempts and invocations requires distinguishing between the workflow definition (intent) and execution instances (runs).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Add an optional keyword-only run_id: str | None = None parameter to run_workflow and run_workflow_from_file.
  2. If run_id is omitted, generate uuid.uuid4().hex.
  3. run_workflow returns the run_id as a string (was None), providing an additive API change.
  4. Record run start and terminal completion in the runs table, including start/finish timestamps, final status, and serialized workflow definition JSON.
  5. Provide query functions get_run_status(conn, run_id) and list_runs(conn, workflow_id=None) returning runs ordered newest first.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Callers can trace specific runs end-to-end.
  • Run status can be queried directly from SQLite even without holding in-memory workflow instances.

docs.title: ADR 006: Crash Recovery and Resume Semantics
Context
docs.text: Long-running workflows (especially multi-step AI pipelines) can experience abrupt process termination (e.g. host reboot, SIGKILL, container eviction). The engine needs to resume execution without re-executing already completed work or leaving tasks stuck in transient states.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Implement resume_run(conn, run_id, task_runner, time_source, *, sleep=time.sleep):
  2. If the run is already in a terminal status (SUCCEEDED or FAILED), return its status immediately without invoking the runner.
  3. Reconstruct the Workflow object by deserializing definition_json stored in the runs record.
  4. Restore each task's latest state, attempt_count, and next_retry_at by scanning task_events for the run.
  5. For any task left in RUNNING status (the process died while running it), treat it as an interrupted attempt: set task.last_error = "interrupted: process exited while running" and invoke fail_task to transition it to RETRY_WAIT or FAILED according to its retry policy.
  6. Resume the normal scheduling loop via run_workflow. Tasks in SUCCEEDED status are never re-executed.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Workflows are fully resilient against unexpected process crashes.
  • Interrupted tasks respect their configured retry policies and failure tracking.

docs.title: ADR 007: Task vs TaskRun Internal Representation
Context
docs.text: A classic architectural decision in workflow orchestrators is whether to introduce a separate TaskRun dataclass representing a specific execution attempt of a Task, or to maintain Task as the state container updated in-place with historical transitions preserved in SQLite.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Retain Task as the primary lifecycle object during execution, rather than introducing a public TaskRun abstraction: 1. Task encapsulates the current in-flight state, attempt_count, and last_error. 2. Every state transition and attempt is immutably logged to task_events tagged with run_id, timestamp, and attempt_count. 3. An internal _run_id attribute on Task links tasks to their run context without widening public constructor contracts. 4. Engine scheduling reads task.state as the single source of truth, eliminating desynchronization between in-memory structures and dictionaries.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The public API surface remains minimal, clean, and backwards-compatible.
  • Detailed execution history is fully preserved in SQLite for querying, replay, and resumption.

docs.title: ADR 008: Single-Writer Coordinator Architecture for Concurrency
Context
docs.text: Adding concurrent task execution introduces concurrency hazards with SQLite (which requires careful cross-thread connection sharing) and risks violating Invariant 1 (write-ahead logging must persist state before mutating in-memory models).

docs.title: Options Considered
docs.text:
1. Multi-Writer Threads: Each worker thread receives a shared or thread-local SQLite connection and performs its own state transitions directly.
  2. Tradeoff: High risk of sqlite3.ProgrammingError, database locks/busy errors, race conditions in status evaluation, and complex distributed state coordination.
  3. Single-Writer Coordinator (Chosen): The main coordinator thread (calling run_workflow) retains sole ownership of:
  4. All state transitions (transition_task).
  5. All SQLite database reads, writes, and migrations.
  6. All scheduling decisions and readiness calculations. Workers (threads or processes) are pure execution engines executing only the user-provided task_runner(task) callable and returning a lightweight completion result (ok: bool, exception: BaseException | None).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Adopt the Single-Writer Coordinator model: - The coordinator maintains an active pool of in-flight tasks up to max_concurrency. - As tasks complete or time out, worker outcomes are returned to the coordinator. - The coordinator performs write-ahead database persistence and advances task lifecycles sequentially. - No SQLite connection is ever passed to or touched by worker threads or child processes.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Invariant 1 (write-ahead log before mutating state) remains strictly preserved.
  • Complete thread-safety and SQLite isolation with zero database contention.
  • Clean separation between execution (user logic) and orchestration (scheduling & persistence).

docs.title: ADR 009: Data Flow, Task Outputs, and Schema v2
Context
docs.text: Orchestrating multi-step AI pipelines and general computational DAGs requires passing data between tasks (e.g. retrieval steps feeding extraction steps). In v0.1.0-v0.4.0, task runners returned a boolean indicating success or failure without returning output data.

docs.title: Options Considered
docs.text:
1. Side-channel shared state / Context object: Pass a mutable shared dictionary or context object to every task runner.
  2. Tradeoff: Prone to race conditions under concurrency, non-deterministic, and breaks isolation between independent branches.
  3. Explicit Dependency Data Flow (TaskResult & Task.inputs) (Chosen):
  4. Task runners can return bool (legacy compatibility) or a frozen TaskResult(ok: bool, output: Any = None, error: str | None = None).
  5. The engine automatically collects outputs from completed dependency tasks and injects them into task.inputs: dict[str, Any] before task dispatch.
  6. Outputs are persisted as JSON in SQLite (task_outputs table) under Schema v2.
  7. On crash or workflow resumption, inputs are reconstructed from persisted outputs.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Introduce TaskResult(ok: bool, output: Any = None, error: str | None = None) in models.py.
  • Add Task.inputs: dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict) as the final field of Task.
  • Upgrade SQLite schema to v2 (PRAGMA user_version = 2), adding task_outputs(run_id, task_id, output_json, error).
  • Require outputs to be JSON-serializable; non-serializable outputs are treated as failed attempts with explanatory last_error rather than crashing the engine.
  • Reconstruct outputs on resume_run so upstream data remains available to downstream tasks after interruptions.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Full backward compatibility: runners returning bool continue to work unchanged.
  • Clean, deterministic data flow with persistent auditability and crash recovery.
  • Safe serialization boundary: prevents storing arbitrary unpicklable objects or breaking database schema.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Users, monitoring systems, and tracing tools need to observe workflow and task lifecycle events (task start, success, failure, retry, workflow completion).

docs.title: Options Considered
docs.text:
1. Interceptor middleware: Allow hooks to intercept and mutate state or abort execution.
  2. Tradeoff: Fragile; user errors in hooks can corrupt state or break engine invariants.
  3. Safe post-persistence event hooks (Chosen):
  4. Hooks are called strictly after matching database transactions and event logging succeed.
  5. Any exception raised inside a hook callable is caught and safely suppressed (logged to standard logging), preventing user hook bugs from interrupting workflow execution or modifying task state.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Introduce Hooks dataclass in models.py with optional callables:
  • on_task_start: Callable[[Task], None] | None = None
  • on_task_succeeded: Callable[[Task], None] | None = None
  • on_task_failed: Callable[[Task], None] | None = None
  • on_task_retry: Callable[[Task], None] | None = None
  • on_workflow_done: Callable[[Workflow, WorkflowStatus], None] | None = None
  • Pass hooks: Hooks | None = None to run_workflow, run_workflow_from_file, and resume_run.
  • Add Hooks to the public API exports in orchestration_engine.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Zero blast radius: raising hooks cannot crash workflows.
  • Clean separation between workflow logic, engine state, and observability.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Defining workflows programmatically via raw dataclass instantiations (Task, RetryPolicy, Workflow) is verbose, error-prone, and doesn't validate DAG properties until execution time. Furthermore, serializing an in-memory Workflow back to standard JSON was not exported.

docs.title: Options Considered
docs.text:
1. Direct dataclass construction only: Keep relying solely on Workflow(...) and Task(...).
  2. Tradeoff: Lacks a fluent API, allows deferred validation errors.
  3. Fluent WorkflowBuilder and workflow_to_dict (Chosen):
  4. WorkflowBuilder: Fluent builder chaining .task(...), .description(...), .build().
  5. Validation upon build: .build() immediately runs DAG validation and raises WorkflowValidationError if dependencies are broken or cycles exist.
  6. workflow_to_dict: Serializes a Workflow into a JSON-compatible dictionary matching the engine schema and round-tripping with load_workflow_from_json.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Implement WorkflowBuilder in src/orchestration_engine/builder.py.
  • Implement workflow_to_dict in src/orchestration_engine/builder.py.
  • Export WorkflowBuilder and workflow_to_dict in orchestration_engine.__all__.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Clean, ergonomic programmatic API for defining workflows in Python.
  • Exact round-trip fidelity between dictionary representations and Workflow domain objects.

docs.title: ADR 012: JSON Schema and Collect-Errors Validation
Context
docs.text: External systems and authoring tools need a formal JSON Schema to validate workflow files ahead of time. Additionally, developer ergonomics are significantly degraded when a loader fails on only one error at a time (forcing multiple compile/run cycles to fix multiple syntax or schema mistakes).

docs.title: Options Considered
docs.text:
1. Third-party schema validation library (e.g. jsonschema):
  2. Tradeoff: Violates the zero-runtime-dependencies core design philosophy.
  3. Built-in JSON Schema asset + native collect-errors validation (Chosen):
  4. Package a formal JSON Schema (src/orchestration_engine/workflow.schema.json) that can be used by external IDEs, YAML/JSON language servers, or test tooling.
  5. Implement load_workflow_from_json(data, *, collect_errors: bool = False) natively in Python standard library.
  6. When collect_errors=False (default): preserve exact fail-fast behavior.
  7. When collect_errors=True: accumulate all definition errors with JSON-pointer paths (e.g. /tasks/0/retry_policy/max_attempts) and raise a single WorkflowDefinitionError with an .errors list.
  8. Ignore unknown keys and allow $schema for forward compatibility.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Ship workflow.schema.json within package data.
  • Add collect_errors: bool = False to load_workflow_from_json.
  • Attach errors: list[str] attribute to WorkflowDefinitionError.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Zero runtime dependencies preserved.
  • Full tooling compatibility and comprehensive validation error reporting in a single pass.

docs.title: ADR 013: Optional YAML Support via PyYAML Extra
Context
docs.text: Many users and workflow authors prefer YAML for human readability. However, parsing YAML requires third-party dependencies (e.g. PyYAML), which would compromise the engine's core zero-runtime-dependency commitment.

docs.title: Options Considered
docs.text:
1. Require PyYAML as a mandatory runtime dependency:
  2. Tradeoff: Violates the zero-runtime-dependencies promise for users only using JSON or Python programmatic builders.
  3. Optional extra orchestration-engine[yaml] with lazy import (Chosen):
  4. Core library remains 100% dependency-free.
  5. Introduce load_workflow_from_yaml which imports yaml lazily on call.
  6. If yaml is missing, raise a clear OrchestrationError instructing the user to install orchestration-engine[yaml].
  7. Always parse with yaml.safe_load to prevent arbitrary code execution vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Add optional dependency yaml = ["pyyaml>=6.0"] in pyproject.toml.
  • Provide load_workflow_from_yaml in loader.py.
  • Export load_workflow_from_yaml in orchestration_engine.__all__.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Core stays dependency-free; users wanting YAML install the optional extra safely.
  • Safe YAML parsing prevents deserialization security attacks.

docs.title: ADR 014: Command-Line Interface and Structured Logging Architecture
Context
docs.text: Operators and automation pipelines require a command-line interface to inspect, validate, run, and resume workflows without writing Python driver scripts. Additionally, observability requires structured logging without imposing unwanted logging configurations on embedded library users.

docs.title: Options Considered
docs.text:
1. Third-party CLI frameworks (e.g. Click, Typer, Rich):
  2. Tradeoff: Violates the zero-runtime-dependencies core design philosophy.
  3. Standard library argparse and logging.NullHandler (Chosen):
  4. Provide CLI entry points via [project.scripts] orchestration-engine = "orchestration_engine.cli:main" and python -m orchestration_engine.
  5. Implement commands: validate, run, resume, status, history, runs.
  6. Contracted exit codes: 0 (succeeded), 1 (workflow failed), 2 (usage/definition error), 3 (internal error).
  7. Stable machine-readable --json output for automation scripts.
  8. Dynamic runner resolution via importlib.import_module with current working directory prepended to sys.path.
  9. Library logger orchestration_engine configured with NullHandler(). Transitions logged at INFO, retries/timeouts at WARNING, database errors at ERROR, with structured extra fields. CLI enables global logging only when --log-level is explicitly provided.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Build orchestration_engine.cli using argparse.
  • Add orchestration_engine/__main__.py.
  • Configure logging.NullHandler() on library logger in __init__.py.
  • Document CLI contracts and exit codes in docs/cli.md.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Zero runtime dependencies maintained.
  • Standardized exit codes and JSON output allow reliable pipeline automation.
  • Safe library logging avoids hijacking client application logging configurations.

The Orchestration Engine has progressed from an initial prototype (v0.1.0) through six complete stages of engineering, hardening, and verification to reach a release-ready v1.0.0. docs.title: 4. Complete List of Behavior Changes (v0.1.0 to v1.0.0)
docs.text:
1. Retry Delay Formula: Delay is calculated relative to the finish timestamp of the failed attempt (attempt_finish_time + delay), preventing instantaneous retries on long-running tasks.
  2. Exception Handling: Unhandled exceptions raised by a task runner are caught, recorded in task.last_error, and handled according to RetryPolicy rather than immediately crashing the workflow coordinator.
  3. Non-blocking Thread Timeouts: Task timeouts terminate execution coordinator wait time without holding the coordinator thread blocked.
  4. Timeout Defaults: Tasks without explicit timeout_seconds inherit workflow.default_timeout_seconds (defaulting to 30.0s). Explicit None disables task timeout.
  5. Transitive Cancellation: If task A fails permanently, all downstream dependents (direct and indirect) transition to CANCELLED within a single scheduling pass.
  6. Persistence Single Source of Truth: task_states dictionary is now a read-only backwards-compatible mirror; the SQLite event log is the authoritative source of truth.
  7. Crash Resume Semantics: Incomplete runs can be safely resumed via resume_run(conn, run_id, ...). Interrupted tasks in RUNNING or RETRY_WAIT state are recovered to READY or re-scheduled.
  8. Multi-Thread & Multi-Process Concurrency: Workflows can execute independent tasks concurrently (max_concurrency > 1) using threads or isolated spawned child processes (multiprocessing).
  9. Data Flow & Task Outputs: Tasks can return TaskResult(ok=True, output=data). Output is persisted in SQLite task_outputs table and passed to downstream tasks via task.inputs = {dep_id: output}.
  10. Lifecycle Hooks: User-provided callbacks (Hooks) trigger on state transitions. Any exceptions inside hooks are caught and logged without aborting task scheduling.
  11. Security Limits: Added maximum file size protection (10 MB), maximum task count (5,000 tasks), and maximum dependency count (500 per task) to guard against resource exhaustion.
  12. CLI Contract: Introduced command-line utility orchestration-engine with strict exit codes (0, 1, 2, 3) and machine-readable JSON mode.

docs.text: All architectural choices are recorded in docs/decisions/: - ADR 001: docs/decisions/001-thread-pool-non-blocking-timeouts.md — Non-blocking timeouts via unpooled executor shutdown. - ADR 002: docs/decisions/002-exception-retry-and-last-error.md — Runner exception capture and retry semantics. - ADR 003: docs/decisions/003-error-hierarchy.md — Domain error hierarchy rooted at OrchestrationError. - ADR 004: docs/decisions/004-schema-v1-and-runs-table.md — Relational schema versioning and runs tracking. - ADR 005: docs/decisions/005-run-model-and-lifecycle.md — Immutable run identification and lifecycle status. - ADR 006: docs/decisions/006-resume-semantics.md — Crash recovery and idempotent resume execution. - ADR 007: docs/decisions/007-task-vs-taskrun-representation.md — Task definition decoupling from run execution states. - ADR 008: docs/decisions/008-single-writer-coordinator-concurrency.md — Single-writer coordinator architecture for concurrent tasks. - ADR 009: docs/decisions/009-data-flow-and-task-outputs.md — TaskResult contract, output persistence, and upstream injection. - ADR 010: docs/decisions/010-hooks-lifecycle.md — Non-blocking post-persistence lifecycle hooks. - ADR 011: docs/decisions/011-workflow-builder-and-serializer.md — Fluent WorkflowBuilder and dictionary round-trip. - ADR 012: docs/decisions/012-json-schema-and-error-collection.md — Packaged JSON Schema and multi-error validation. - ADR 013: docs/decisions/013-optional-yaml-support.md — Zero-dependency core with optional PyYAML loader. - ADR 014: docs/decisions/014-cli-and-structured-logging.md — Standard library CLI contract and NullHandler logging.

docs.title: 6. Intentionally Out-of-Scope Items
docs.text: To preserve the engine's core promise of zero runtime dependencies, minimal surface area, and rock-solid durability, the following capabilities are explicitly out of scope for v1.0.0: 1. Distributed Multi-Node Execution: No distributed worker pools (e.g. Celery, Ray, Kubernetes). All concurrency is single-node multi-thread or multi-process. 2. External Message Brokers / Databases: No dependency on Redis, RabbitMQ, Kafka, or PostgreSQL. Persistence is strictly standard library SQLite. 3. Web UI / Graphical Dashboard: No bundled web server (e.g. Flask, FastAPI, React). Monitoring is accomplished via SQLite queries, the CLI (orchestration-engine status / history), or application logs. 4. Dynamic DAG Mutation at Runtime: The task graph is fully declared before execution starts; dynamic graph topology expansion during run execution is not supported.

docs.title: 7. Known Technical Limitations
docs.text:
1. Thread Backend Cancellation: The executor="thread" backend uses standard Python concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor. In Python, running native threads cannot be forcefully terminated from the outside. When a threaded task times out, the engine stops waiting and proceeds with workflow scheduling, but the worker thread will run until completion or interpreter exit. For tasks that must be forcefully terminated on timeout, use executor="process".
  2. SQLite Single-Writer Concurrency: While SQLite in WAL mode permits concurrent readers, it enforces a single writer lock. Under the single-writer coordinator pattern, this is completely safe within an engine instance. Multiple independent processes pointing to the exact same SQLite database file should rely on the configured busy_timeout (default 5000ms).

docs.title: 2. Path and Runner Trust Model
docs.text:
• Finding: The --runner module:function CLI option dynamically imports user modules and executes Python code.
  • Remediation: The security boundary is explicitly documented in SECURITY.md, docs/cli.md, and inline docstrings. Executing --runner carries the same trust model as executing an arbitrary Python script. Operators must restrict input to trusted runner paths.

docs.title: 3. Safe Loading for Definitions (JSON & YAML)
docs.text:
• JSON Loading: Standard json.loads is used. Unknown fields are ignored during execution to ensure forward compatibility, while collect_errors=True checks standard JSON schema types.
  • YAML Loading: Only yaml.safe_load is utilized in loader.py. Arbitrary Python object deserialization via YAML tags is prohibited. Verified via tests/test_security.py::test_yaml_safe_load_blocks_arbitrary_code.

docs.title: 4. Size, Depth, and Resource Exhaustion Limits
docs.text:
• Workflow File Size: Enforced limit of 10 MB (MAX_WORKFLOW_FILE_SIZE). Files exceeding 10 MB are rejected immediately before reading or parsing. Verified via tests/test_security.py::test_file_size_limit_json.
  • Workflow Task Count: Enforced limit of 5,000 tasks (MAX_TASKS_PER_WORKFLOW). Verified via tests/test_security.py::test_workflow_task_count_limit.
  • Task Dependencies Count: Enforced limit of 500 dependencies per task (MAX_DEPENDENCIES_PER_TASK). Verified via tests/test_security.py::test_task_dependencies_count_limit.

docs.title: 5. Pickle Serialization Scope
docs.text:
• Audit: pickle usage was audited across the entire codebase.
  • Result: pickle is used exclusively in src/orchestration_engine/runner.py for IPC over unidirectional pipes in multiprocessing.get_context("spawn"). It is never used for database persistence, file loading, or thread execution.

docs.title: 6. Supply Chain & Dependencies
docs.text:
• Core Runtime Dependencies: 0 (zero runtime third-party dependencies).
  • Development Tooling: Development dependencies (mypy, pytest, pytest-cov, ruff, pyyaml, mkdocs, mkdocs-material) are pinned and managed strictly via pyproject.toml and locked in uv.lock.
